headline: A scan error says which error it was
summary: `b.mail.scan` on the clamav-instream backend answered every failure with `{ verdict: "error", threats: [] }` and nothing else, so a message too large for the daemon to scan and a daemon that was down arrived identically. A refusal on size will never succeed on retry and a fault clears when the daemon returns, so the two call for different handling. Error verdicts now carry `errorCode` and `errorMessage`.

items.title: `errorCode` and `errorMessage` on a clamav-instream error verdict
items.body:
An error verdict from the clamav-instream backend now names which error it was. `mail-scan/clamav-size-limit` is a stream past the daemon's `StreamMaxLength`, which depends on the size of the message and will not succeed on retry. `mail-scan/clamav-error` is a daemon fault, which clears when the daemon returns. `mail-scan/clamav-unparsed-reply` is a reply the framework could not classify as any of clean, infected or error.

`errorMessage` carries the daemon's own words for the failure, truncated to 200 characters because the length of that reply is the daemon's to choose.

The fields are additive and the `verdict` values are unchanged, so a caller that branches on `verdict` alone behaves as before. The ICAP backend already returned the parsed response with its status code, and a scan that threw already set `errorCode`; the clamav-instream resolutions were the only ones answering with nothing.

items.title: A clamd reply that arrives before a reset is kept
items.body:
clamd closes the connection as soon as a stream passes `StreamMaxLength`, while the framework is still writing chunks, so the size-limit reply can be followed by a connection reset with no clean end. The reply was read only on a clean end, so on that path it was discarded and the caller received `mail-scan/transport` for a message the daemon had already answered about, which invites the retry the size-limit code exists to prevent.

A reply that arrived is now used whatever the socket does next, on one condition: clamd terminates a reply with a NUL or a newline, and only a terminated reply is read. Bytes a reset cut in half stay a transport failure, because `stream: OK.` is also the start of an infected reply whose signature name begins `OK.`, and reading it as clean would report a clean scan of a message that was never fully scanned.

The ICAP backend deliberately does not do this. An ICAP response declares an encapsulated body length that the parser does not check against the bytes present, so headers followed by a reset would parse as a complete clean response. A reset ICAP scan stays a transport failure.
